unit: Ch 4: Income of Other Persons included in Total Income of Assessee
note: AI-written summary of ICAI study material. Check the original for exact wording.

topics.title: Introduction to Clubbing & Transfer of Income Without Transfer of Asset
explain: Income tax is progressive, so taxpayers try to shift income to family members to lower their tax slab.
To prevent tax evasion, clubbing provisions add income earned by others back into the transferor's total income.
If you transfer the right to receive income from an asset without transferring ownership of the asset itself, that income is clubbed with your income.
It does not matter whether the transfer is revocable or irrevocable, or made before or after the Act.

flow.title: Transfer of Income Without Asset
steps: Asset owned by Transferor
Transferor transfers income rights only
Transferee receives the income
Apply Section 96 Clubbing Rule
Income taxed in hands of Transferor

topics.example: Mr. A transfers the right to receive rent from his house property to his wife without transferring ownership of the house. The rental income will still be taxed in Mr. A's hands.
remember: Section 96 applies when income is transferred without transferring the underlying asset.
Ownership remains with the transferor.
mistakes: Thinking that an irrevocable transfer of income without asset avoids clubbing.

quiz.q: Mr. Vatsan transfers rental income from a godown to his son via a registered document without transferring the godown itself. In whose hands is the rental income taxable?
quiz.why: Under Section 96, transfer of income without transferring the asset results in income being clubbed in the hands of the transferor.

quiz.q: Does Section 96 apply if the transfer of income without asset is irrevocable?
o: No, it only applies to revocable transfers
Yes, it is immaterial whether the transfer is revocable or irrevocable
Only if approved by the Assessing Officer
Only if the transferee is a minor
quiz.why: Section 96 applies regardless of whether the transfer of income is revocable or irrevocable.

topics.title: Income from Revocable Transfer of Assets & Exceptions
explain: A transfer is revocable if it allows direct or indirect re-transfer of asset/income to the transferor, or gives power to re-assume control over it.
Income arising from a revocable transfer of assets is clubbed in the hands of the transferor under Section 97(1).
Even if only a part of the income is used for the transferor's benefit, the entire income from the asset is clubbed.

Under Section 97(2), clubbing does NOT apply if the transfer is by trust not revocable during beneficiary's lifetime, or any other transfer not revocable during transferee's lifetime, provided the transferor gets no direct/indirect benefit.
As soon as the power to revoke arises, the income is clubbed with the transferor's total income.

flow.title: Testing Revocable Transfer Clubbing
steps: Asset transferred to another person
Is transfer revocable during transferee lifetime?
If Yes: Club income under Section 97(1)
If No: Check if transferor gets any benefit
If benefit derived: Club income in transferor hands
If no benefit: Tax in hands of transferee until revocation power arises

topics.example: Mr. Rajesh transfers house property to a trust for Mr. Ramesh until Ramesh dies. This is irrevocable during Ramesh's lifetime. Income is taxed to the trust until Ramesh dies; after his death, it becomes revocable and taxable to Rajesh.
remember: Re-transfer provisions or power to re-assume control makes a transfer revocable.
Section 97(2) protects irrevocable transfers during lifetime of beneficiary/transferee only if transferor derives zero benefit.
mistakes: Assuming partial benefit to transferor means only partial clubbing; once revocable, the entire income is clubbed.

quiz.q: Under Section 98, a transfer is deemed revocable if:
o: It is made without any monetary consideration
It contains a provision for re-transfer of asset or income to transferor
It is made to a spouse under an agreement to live apart
It is made to a minor child who is disabled
quiz.why: A transfer is revocable if it contains any provision for re-transfer or right to re-assume power over the asset or income.

quiz.q: Mr. X transfers an asset under a revocable arrangement to Mr. Y. The income from the asset is taxable in the hands of:
o: Both Mr. X and Mr. Y equally
quiz.why: Income from a revocable transfer of assets is clubbed in the hands of the transferor (Mr. X) under Section 97(1).

topics.title: Remuneration to Spouse from Concern with Substantial Interest
explain: Any salary, commission, fees or remuneration paid to a spouse from a concern where the individual has a substantial interest is clubbed in the individual's income.
Substantial interest means holding 20% or more voting power in a company, or 20% or more share in profits of a non-company concern, owned by the individual along with relatives.
'Relative' under Section 2(94) includes husband, wife, brother, sister, lineal ascendant, or lineal descendant.
EXCEPTION: No clubbing if the remuneration is solely attributable to the spouse's technical or professional knowledge, experience, or qualifications.

If BOTH husband and wife have substantial interest and both get remuneration without professional qualifications, the remuneration is clubbed with the spouse whose income (before such inclusion) is higher.

flow.title: Spouse Remuneration Clubbing Logic
steps: Spouse receives salary/remuneration from concern
Check if individual (with relatives) holds 20%+ interest
If No substantial interest: Tax in spouse hands
If Yes: Check if spouse has professional/technical qualification
If Qualified: Tax in spouse hands (No clubbing)
If Unqualified: Club remuneration in individual's hands

topics.example: Mr. A holds 25% voting power in X (P) Ltd. Mrs. A works there as a software programmer earning ₹2,85,000 without any relevant qualification. Her salary is clubbed in Mr. A's hands.
remember: Substantial interest benchmark threshold is 20%.
Professional qualification exception prevents clubbing.
Once clubbed in one spouse's hands, it cannot be shifted to the other in subsequent years unless AO is satisfied after giving hearing.
mistakes: Clubbing remuneration even when the spouse possesses genuine technical qualifications required for the job.

quiz.q: What is the threshold of voting power required for an individual (together with relatives) to have a substantial interest in a company?
quiz.why: Substantial interest in a company requires holding equity shares carrying 20% or more voting power at any time during the tax year.

quiz.q: If both husband and wife have substantial interest in a firm and both earn salary without technical qualifications, where is the salary clubbed?
o: In the hands of the spouse whose total income before inclusion is higher
quiz.why: Where both have substantial interest and earn unqualified remuneration, it is clubbed with the spouse having higher income before such inclusion.

topics.title: Transferred Assets to Spouse & Son's Wife
explain: If an asset (other than house property) is transferred to spouse or son's wife directly/indirectly without adequate consideration, income from that asset is clubbed in the transferor's hands.

If house property is transferred to spouse without adequate consideration, Section 25(a) applies: transferor is deemed owner, so annual value is taxed directly in transferor's hands (not under clubbing).
Natural love and affection do NOT constitute adequate consideration.
No clubbing applies if transfer to spouse is in connection with an agreement to live apart.

If transferred asset is invested in business/firm by spouse or son's wife, proportionate income is clubbed using formula: Income = B × (C / D), where B = business profit/interest, C = transferred asset invested on 1st day of tax year, D = total investment on 1st day of tax year.
Income from accretion of transferred asset (e.g. interest on interest) is NOT clubbed.

flow.title: Asset Transferred to Spouse / Son's Wife
steps: Asset transferred to Spouse or Son's Wife
Was consideration adequate or for living apart?
If Adequate/Living apart: Tax in transferee hands
If Inadequate and House Property: Deemed owner u/s 25(a)
If Inadequate and Other Asset: Club income u/s 99(1)(a)(ii) or 99(1)(b)
If invested in business: Apply Proportionate Formula A = B × (C/D)

topics.example: Mr. X transfers debentures of ₹1,00,000 earning ₹12,000 interest to his wife without consideration. The ₹12,000 interest is clubbed with Mr. X. If she re-invests ₹12,000 to earn ₹960, the ₹960 interest on accretion is taxable in her hands.
remember: Natural love and affection is NOT adequate consideration.
Accretion of income is not subject to clubbing.
Proportionate formula B × (C/D) considers values on the 1st day of the tax year.
mistakes: Applying clubbing provisions to income earned from investing the accumulated income (accretion) of the transferred asset.

quiz.q: Rohan transferred 2,000 shares to Ms. Neha without consideration. Later, they got married. Is dividend income from these shares clubbed after marriage?
o: Yes, taxable in Rohan's hands both before and after marriage
Taxable in Rohan's hands before marriage but not after
Taxable in Rohan's hands after marriage but not before marriage
Not taxable in Rohan's hands either before or after marriage
quiz.why: Relationship of spouse must exist both at the time of transfer of asset and at the time of accrual of income. Thus, after marriage it is clubbed in Rohan's hands.

quiz.q: What happens if a house property is gifted by an individual to their spouse without adequate consideration (and not to live apart)?
o: Transferor is deemed owner under Section 25(a)
Income is taxed in the hands of the spouse
quiz.why: For house property transferred to spouse without adequate consideration, Section 25(a) deems the transferor to be the owner, so Section 99(1)(a)(ii) does not apply.

topics.title: Clubbing of Minor Child's Income & Exemptions
explain: All income of a minor child is clubbed in the hands of the parent whose total income (excluding minor's income) is higher.
If parents' marriage does not subsist, income is clubbed in the hands of the parent who maintains the minor child.
EXCEPTIONS (No Clubbing): 1) Income from manual work done by minor, 2) Income from minor's skill, talent, or specialized knowledge, 3) Minor child suffering from disability u/s 154.
EXEMPTION: Parent can claim exemption up to ₹1,500 per minor child under Schedule III (Table: S. No. 17) ONLY IF the parent shifts out of the default tax regime.
Under the default tax regime (section 202(1)), the ₹1,500 exemption per minor child is NOT available.
Child includes step-child and adopted child.

flow.title: Minor Child Income Clubbing Process
steps: Minor child earns income
Check Exceptions: Manual work, skill/talent, or Sec 154 disability?
If Exception applies: Tax directly in minor's hands
If No Exception: Club in hands of parent with higher income
Check Tax Regime of parent
If Shifted out of Default Regime: Deduct exemption up to ₹1,500 per child
If Default Regime: Include full income without ₹1,500 exemption

topics.example: Minor daughter C earns ₹32,000 from classical dance (special talent) and ₹3,000 bank interest. The ₹32,000 is taxed in C's hands. The ₹3,000 bank interest is clubbed with father Mr. A (higher income parent). If Mr. A opts out of default regime, net clubbed income is ₹1,500 (₹3,000 - ₹1,500).
remember: Exemption limit is up to ₹1,500 per minor child.
₹1,500 exemption is available ONLY under non-default regime.
Bank interest on savings from talent income IS clubbed.
mistakes: Exempting bank interest earned on deposits created out of minor's talent/skill income.

quiz.q: Ms. Priya, a minor child, earned ₹40,000 from dance performances and ₹5,000 as bank interest on deposits created from dance earnings. Which statement is correct?
o: Entire ₹45,000 is taxable in Priya's hands
Entire ₹45,000 is clubbed in parent's hands
₹40,000 is taxable in Priya's hands and ₹5,000 is clubbed in parent's hands
Entire income is exempt from tax
quiz.why: Income from talent (₹40,000) is taxed in minor's hands, but interest earned on investment of such income (₹5,000) is clubbed with the parent.

quiz.q: Is the exemption of up to ₹1,500 per child under Schedule III available under the default tax regime?
o: No, it is available only if the parent shifts out of the default tax regime
Yes, but only for disabled children
quiz.why: The ₹1,500 exemption under Schedule III (Table: S. No. 17) is not available under the default tax regime.

topics.title: Assets Transferred for Benefit of Spouse / Son's Wife & Cross Transfers
explain: If an individual transfers an asset without adequate consideration to any person or AOP for the immediate or deferred benefit of spouse or son's wife, income from such asset is clubbed with the individual.
Cross Transfers: Circuitous transactions created to evade tax (e.g. A gifts to B's wife, B gifts to A's minor son) are treated as interconnected single transactions (CIT v. Keshavji Morarji).
In cross transfers, each transferor is deemed an indirect transferor to their own spouse/child to the extent of matching consideration.
Income from cross-transferred assets is clubbed in the hands of the deemed transferor up to the matching cross-transfer amount.

flow.title: Cross Transfer Clubbing Logic
steps: A gifts asset to B's relative
Simultaneously B gifts asset to A's relative
Identify inter-connected device to evade tax
Determine matching cross-transfer amount
Deem A and B as indirect transferors to own relative
Club income in respective deemed transferors' hands

topics.example: Mr. Vasudevan gifts ₹6 lakhs to his brother's wife, and his brother gifts ₹5 lakhs to Mrs. Vasudevan. Interest on ₹5 lakhs (matching amount) earned by Mrs. Vasudevan is clubbed in Mr. Vasudevan's hands.
remember: Section 99(1)(d) covers transfers to third parties/AOPs for benefit of spouse/son's wife.
Cross transfers are clubbed to the extent of equal/matching amounts exchanged.
mistakes: Clubbing the entire income when cross transfer amounts are unequal, instead of restricting clubbing to the lower matching amount.

quiz.q: Mr. A gifts ₹5 lakhs to B's wife, while B simultaneously gifts ₹5 lakhs to Mr. A's wife. Both invest in bank deposits. This arrangement is known as:
quiz.why: Inter-connected mutual transfers to bypass clubbing rules are classified as cross transfers, and income is clubbed with the deemed transferor.

quiz.q: Mrs. Kasturi transfers property to ABC Co. Ltd. on the condition that ₹36,000 p.a. of rental income be used for her son's wife. In whose hands is ₹36,000 taxable?
quiz.why: Under Section 99(1)(d), income from asset transferred for benefit of son's wife is clubbed in the hands of the transferor (Mrs. Kasturi).

topics.title: Conversion of Self-Acquired Property into HUF Property
explain: If an individual converts self-acquired property into HUF property (by throwing it into common stock or transferring without adequate consideration), income from such property continues to be clubbed in the individual's income.
On partition of the HUF, the converted property is divided among members.
Income derived from converted property received by the spouse on partition is deemed to arise from an indirect transfer by the individual and is clubbed in the individual's hands u/s 99(1)(a).
Income received by minor children on partition is clubbed u/s 99(1)(c) with the parent having higher income.
Income received by major sons/daughters on partition is taxed in their own respective hands.

flow.title: Conversion of Property to HUF & Partition
steps: Individual converts self-acquired property to HUF property
Before Partition: Entire annual income clubbed in individual's hands
HUF Partition occurs
Individual's own share: Taxed in individual's hands
Spouse's share: Clubbed with individual u/s 99(1)(a)
Minor child's share: Clubbed u/s 99(1)(c) with parent of higher income
Major child's share: Taxed directly in major child's hands

topics.example: Mr. Amit converts self-acquired property into HUF property (income ₹1,00,000). Entire ₹1,00,000 is clubbed with Mr. Amit. On partition among Amit, wife, minor son, and major son (₹25,000 each): Mrs. A's ₹25,000 and minor son's ₹25,000 (less ₹1,500 if non-default) are clubbed with Mr. Amit. Major son pays tax on his ₹25,000.
remember: Conversion to HUF does not escape clubbing.
Spouse's partitioned share remains clubbed with the transferor.
Major child's partitioned share is NOT clubbed.
mistakes: Clubbing the share of income received by a major child after HUF partition.

quiz.q: Mr. R converted his self-acquired property into HUF property. On partition, his minor daughter received a share producing income of ₹20,000. If Mr. R's income is higher than Mrs. R's, such income is:
o: Includible in the income of Mr. R
Includible in the income of Mrs. R
quiz.why: After partition, minor daughter's income from converted HUF property is clubbed with the parent earning higher income (Mr. R).

quiz.q: When self-acquired property converted into HUF property is partitioned, how is the share of income received by a major son taxed?
o: Clubbed in the hands of the Karta
Clubbed in the hands of the father/transferor
Taxed directly in the hands of the major son
quiz.why: Clubbing provisions do not apply to major children; the income is taxed directly in the major son's hands.

topics.title: Income Includes Loss & Key Sectional Distinctions
explain: Under Section 99(5)(d), 'income' includes 'loss'.
If a transferred asset generates a loss, that loss will also be clubbed and set off while computing the transferor's total income.
Distinction between Sections 96/97 and Section 99: Section 97 applies only to revocable transfers made by ANY person/assessee.
Section 99 applies to both revocable and irrevocable transfers made ONLY by INDIVIDUALS.
Clubbing applies to income arising directly/indirectly from transferred assets, but NOT to income from accretion (except for minor child's income).

flow.title: Scope & Coverage Comparison
steps: Check Assessee Type & Transfer Nature
If Any Assessee + Revocable Transfer: Apply Sec 97
If Individual + Inadequate Consideration Transfer: Apply Sec 99
Check outcome (Profit or Loss)
If Loss: Club loss in transferor's hands u/s 99(5)(d)
Check accretion: Do NOT club income from accretion

topics.example: Nishant gifts ₹10 lakhs to wife Nisha, who invests it in a business and incurs a loss of ₹15,000. As income includes loss, the ₹15,000 loss is clubbed in Nishant's total income.
remember: Clubbing applies to negative income (losses) too.
Sections 96 and 97 apply to 'any assessee', whereas Section 99 applies strictly to 'individuals'.
mistakes: Refusing to club a business loss incurred by a spouse from funds gifted by the individual.

quiz.q: If a spouse incurs a loss from a business funded entirely by gifted money from the individual, how is the loss treated?
o: Carried forward only by the spouse
Includible/clubbed in the total income of the individual
quiz.why: Under Section 99(5)(d), income includes loss, so loss from transferred assets is clubbed in the transferor's hands.

quiz.q: Which section applies to revocable transfers made by ANY assessee (not limited to individuals)?
quiz.why: Section 97 applies to revocable transfers of assets made by any assessee, whereas Section 99 applies exclusively to individuals.
